On worst-case latency, dense_hash_map is far worse than std::unordered_map (max 689,846 ns vs 10,299 ns in cache; 226,083,255 ns vs 22,422 ns out of cache), so only the mean favors it. sparsehash's own doc/performance.html (2004, gcc 2.95.3 -g -O2, Pentium 4) compares against the SGI hash_map, not std::unordered_map. Its src/time_hash_map.cc can also time the native unordered_map, but the repo publishes no such results. sparsepp's bench.md notes that dense_hash_map ran out of memory at 70M entries because of resize memory spikes. tier_reason: The Verstable README links the results page, and the page links the benchmark code repo JacksonAllan/c_cpp_hash_tables_benchmark (main.cpp, shims/verstable, shims/std_unordered_map). The page states the compiler (GCC 13.2.0 via MinGW-w64), flags (-O3 -DNDEBUG), and hardware (Ryzen 7 5800H at 90% locked frequency).

corrections.claimed_speedup: No numeric multiplier in the text (results are interactive charts). The page's analysis says std::unordered_map is 'far slower than most of the open-addressing tables in most of the benchmarks, except in the case of looking up existing keys, wherein its performance is comparable to that of the slowest open-addressing tables', with iteration 'at least an order of magnitude slower'. Verstable has fast lookups (among the fastest for integer keys with large buckets), 'extremely fast' lookups and erasures of nonexisting keys, and iteration beaten only by boost::unordered_flat_map, emilib2 and contiguous-storage tables, but insertion speed that is 'only average'.

notes: The original claim that Verstable 'falls behind SIMD tables such as absl and boost' overgeneralizes: the page says Verstable iterates faster than absl::flat_hash_map. The 'numbers' are charts, not text. Metadata checks out: MIT, 208 stars, last commit 2025-05-06, stale.

tier_reason: The paper is peer-reviewed (EuroSys'14, DOI 10.1145/2592798.2592820) and the libcuckoo README cites it. Figure 1 (4-core i7-4770, 120M keys, 64-bit key/value, 1:1 read/write) and Figure 2 include C++11 std::unordered_map. The abstract states the ~40M insert / ~70M lookup per second figures on 16 cores and the 'up to 2.5x' figure versus other concurrent tables. The repo's own universal-benchmark supports only LIBCUCKOO, so it is not A.

corrections.caveats: The repo's universal-benchmark (tests/universal-benchmark) compiles only LIBCUCKOO, with no std::unordered_map baseline. The std comparison comes from the EuroSys'14 paper's Figures 1-2, where the multiplier is only visual. The only explicit numeric speedup ('up to 2.5x') is against other concurrent tables such as Intel TBB. The paper treats std::unordered_map as a single-writer table: Section 2.3 says such tables 'allow only one writer at a time', and Figure 2 runs it under a global lock or TSX lock elision. So the win shows multi-core scalability, not a faster single-threaded operation. The compiler, flags, and std library are not stated in the paper.

notes: The quotes and hardware match the paper. GitHub reports the license spdx_id as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the Apache License 2.0 (Carnegie Mellon University and Intel, 2013). The only third-party code is the bundled PCG headers in tests/pcg, so license Apache-2.0 and usability copyable stand. Other metadata checks out: 1747 stars, last commit 2026-07-31.
